commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether keeping training records and auditing completion reduces undetected training gaps, and no study documents the size of the hazard. Four sources endorse the practice, two frameworks and two commentaries, all on the basis of expert judgment and regulatory alignment.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. The four endorsements are frameworks and commentaries, which GRADE treats as expert opinion rather than evidence. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence until a comparative study measures training gaps with and without tracking.

Two commentaries tie training documentation to European requirements, and one cites the AI Act's traceability expectation of recording who was trained, by whom, on which tools, and at what competency level. For systems subject to such rules, record keeping may serve compliance purposes whether or not its effect on patient outcomes has been measured.

commentary.research_gap: No study measures how often AI training gaps occur in health systems, whether completion tracking and periodic audits detect them, or whether detected gaps relate to errors in AI-assisted care. A useful study would compare units with and without tracking and audits on training completion rates, competency assessment results, and AI-related safety events, and would report the staff time the tracking requires.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems may have fewer staff to maintain training records, and any future evaluation would need to include them to show whether the practice is feasible and useful in those settings.
